So they asked me, he says, when my job finished, you see, when my job finished, they asked me if I wanted to stay in my room. I said, sure, and that was luck, you know, and I didn't want to go back to the state, you know. That was really jammed up in my king. I said, I jump on it, I said, sure, because he says, you see, we can't have him, Charlie, and so far, because his wife had already sent him a ticket, you know, the money for him to come back to New Orleans, and he took that money and drank it up. And so he didn't go, because he didn't have the money, so she, Frank wrote to his wife, said, send him a ticket, don't send him the money. So she wired him a ticket, and he couldn't sell it, or he had to use it, or leave it. And so he went back. That's how I took his place, you see.
How was the reception for your type of music? Good.
Well, yes, the people liked it, and while we was waiting at the influence there was more or less Americans, Canadians, and German, French.
There wasn't any color bullshit at that time, was there?
No, not there in Mexico.
You guys really had some experiences on those tours. I was thinking of that one, did you know Gert Morant? No, I haven't.
I knew him. I heard of him.

But you know, he and Octave Crosby went down to Yucatan, about that time you were in Tampico, I think. And, my God, they went nuts over me. They took this wood-burning train, you know, at the small tracks, back to the capital there, Medina. And the Yucatan Spanish made pictures of him and everything else. So there's film shorts of that somewhere. And they came back with $300 and gold.
Yes, that was gold. They didn't have no paper in Mexico. It was all gold. Everything was gold.
So that was something to get down there, then?

Yes. I was, I saved so much money. I was young. I didn't know what to do with it. And Frank and his brother, they made me save some, they taught me to save. And my mother was sick at the time. And I had to send my salary home and keep my tips. Was that good? The tips, the salary was nothing next to the tips because the salary was $2.50 a day from 7 to 5 in the morning. That's $2.50. I was getting five pesos a day at that time. But we didn't make twice that much or much more than that on tips. Oh, yeah. So I'd send my salary to have my father with my mother and keep the tips. And that's how after two years, I felt myself becoming a man, although I wasn't. Not even here. But, you know, getting taller all the time and looking above everybody, especially in Mexico, the man's all short. And the Manti brothers, too, were short fellas. Didn't have five foot, something like that.
What was the name of that joint? Frank?
Uh, Tivoli.
Tivoli. Tivoli. Yeah, Tivoli.

Tivoli. Well, and so I saved so much money. And I used to buy those different magazines in Mexico just to keep myself reading in English. Oh, yeah. And I read in some magazine about the bands that was in Europe. You see, in the Noble Sister, I think. Yeah. You record it. The Man Cook, the Man Cook, Wilman Cook was over, and Louie Mitchell was over there. And the old Pabr group of Breaktown was over. I heard a lot of those people back in, in, in, being in Europe. And how Europe was jumping. Yeah. So, I had saved so much money. I didn't know what to do with it. I said, I'm going to take a trip over there. And, uh, I had to have a passport. Well, I had so much trouble getting my birth certificate right. I almost had given up. My name wasn't right. You know, and everything else in it never got straight. Yeah. That's fast. But I finally did get my name straight. They wanted to make me G-W-D-Y, in which my name was G-O-U-D-I-E.
Yeah.

I have a French name, and it's, it's my name, and I wanted it. You know. And they, they changed my first name, because my first name is Francis. Right. They called me Frank, so I took Frank. It's the same family with Francis.
The, uh, the European boys spelled it G-O-O-D-I-E, didn't they?

Well, they, because they picture it in English. Yeah. You see? They said that English is G-O-U-G down below. They, they don't, they don't realize it's a French name. They use G-O-U. Yeah. In French, if you pronounce G-O-O, it wouldn't sound the same as in English. Oh, it does. Yeah. So they don't think about that. They say, I'm an American, it should be spelled that way. But I'm an American born French, that's all I know about.
Well, what time was it that you were in the city of New Orleans itself?
Well, and after, you know, between the time that I was in Houston. Oh, yeah. You see? And Mexico.
Houston and Mexico?
Before I went to Mexico.
Yeah.
So I played the, I can't call his name. He was looking for me not too long ago, a saxophone player. Had a band from Houston and we went on excursion there.
Oh, yeah.
And I...
Was his first name Earl? No. No. You know, Sam Morgan, the sax player, Earl Fouché?
Mm-hmm.
He's down in Santa Barbara with the New Orleans style band now.
But this guy, he doesn't play no more.
Oh, yeah.
He doesn't play. It's your life. About two weeks ago, he asked for me. I've forgotten his name. But anyway, I went to New Orleans. I worked with Mudd Carrier's brother.
Jack?
Jack Carrier and the other one that plays bass. Jack Carrier was something, wasn't he? Yes. And I played also with, you know this bass player named One Eye Ollie?
Yeah.
I played with him in New Orleans. And then I came back, went back to Houston. And that's, you know, during that time I was waiting around.
Is this when you lived pretty near George himself? George Lewis?

Well, that's how I played, you know, across the street from him. I forgot the name of the place. But when I saw George, hey, you remember the name of the place. We talk a lot. And so that's how, I mean, I went to New Orleans. And then when I left Mexico on my way to Europe, I spent a month. And I played with all those guys again that I knew. Oh, yeah. One month or six weeks. That was the last time I was in New Orleans. And I went across.
This was about 24, 25?
Just about the May month of June, 1924. In fact, I remember right. 1924. For sure it was 1924, more or less June, May, June, something.
Oh, yeah. All this time, I mean, you were picking up on as much music as you could. I mean, uh... Yes.

Well, you see, I had that two years, started working in Mexico with those Matthew Brothers, which was good musicians. They taught me how to transpose, I mean, how to read and how to transpose music. You see, because we couldn't get the orchestration over there in Mexico. We couldn't get, receive those piano parts. And then they taught me how to read piano parts without writing, write a trumpet part.
Yeah.

Just transpose it. And I've got a lot of knowledge from Frank. And that two years or two years and a half experience with him, you see. So when I went to New Orleans, I was already had improved a lot. You were still playing trumpet, right? Yes. And I had already picked up them finally at the little house, you know. And they really wanted me to stay in New Orleans because I could read fairly good, you see, and all that. And all those guys were sleeping going now, you see.

Oh, yeah. And they needed something to play in New Orleans at that time. Morton wasn't even around then, I guess. He was gone. He wasn't even seen. Gleason wrote in one of the notes, you know, on that, the Django Reinhardt LP. Mm-hmm. Did you study under T.O.? Is that so?
Well, I, you know, he made a mistake there. I didn't.
Yeah.

I did. But I figured you would have mentioned it if you hadn't. Yes. No, I didn't because I studied with clarinet in Europe. Oh, yeah. You see, because I had just. You played strictly natural clarinet then when you were in New Orleans. Well, when I was faking, you know, trying to play by ear, but I couldn't do it. I never did play it. Oh, yeah. No, I never did play it. I had it, you know, for myself.
You played trumpet with groups like Caries.
I played trumpet at that time. I never took clarinet out on the job.
Oh, yeah.
The reason I really picked up clarinet, I wanted to, I mean, Freddie Kemper played clarinet. Oh, yeah. And that's the sense he.
Play trumpet with clarinet.
And I picked up, took up, bought a clarinet on a kind of that.
Because I haven't faking never forgot that. Was he something else on clarinet, too?
Well, you know, he knew the instrument and he could play. But he was a solid trumpet player.

Oh. That he had. Even on those old primitive records, his power is fantastic. He was, he was, he was terrific. You say he was the best hot trumpet you've heard? Yes, and with power, you know, hit. Norman told me that it wasn't the kind that hurt your ears.
It just went through the roof.
No, no.

It wasn't a blasting, loud trumpet player. You know, those guys, they had knowledge of the instrument. Yeah. They had knowledge of the instrument. They played it, they played the, well, I can't say the word in English. They played it with the intelligence of the instrument.
Yeah.
They didn't, they didn't overblow and blast out of the note. They just played with indivility of the instrument.
There's so much ignorance, willfulness of those men. I mean, we think we can play on their stupidity. They weren't stupid. They were musicians. No.

No, they're just the people of today. The registration is different from that time and today. It's better to then than it was then. And people just misjudge guys like Mud Carrey, Freddie Caput, and I would say also Spider, which he didn't continue to play. And I've had the opportunity to hear Kid Punch when I was in New Orleans then.
Oh, you heard Punch then. Yeah.
And Punch was just, I mean, he was, it was crazy. But he was doing so much. Those guys, like, I never met a senior at all. I met Dodd. I met Benny Bigard.
Did you meet Dodds when he was playing with Ori?
Yes. And I met Nicholas. People have a wrong conception of those guys. They think they were fakers.
Did Nick remember you from those days?
No, I never, no. I just wondered if you ran across him. I was too young. I don't think he's, I don't know how old he is, but he's not too old.
No. He's in beautiful condition, too. He's in beautiful condition. Did you play with Celestan?
No. You didn't? No. But I heard him play. I heard him play in New Orleans. And you heard Paul Barnes? Oh.
Yeah.

Ridgely? The only one I never heard was P-Roll. It was when I went to Norland for 24 years in Chicago. Oh, yeah. I didn't get to hear. And he had a bunch of nice musicians with him. And I really wanted to hear, but I didn't get a chance.
Which, let's see, that would have been around after the war. See, that would have been probably from 20 to 23, wouldn't it? I'd say. Or 19. 1919 to 22 in there when you were in New Orleans.
Well, no, no, it was, it would have been 20. 20. 20.
Yes. Yeah, because John Dodds hadn't left yet. Johnny Dodds hadn't left there yet.
Well, 20 would have left there.
Boy, I guess it's just as fantastic as they say it was.

I think he can see him settling down in Eli Cabaret as if it was yesterday. He was playing. Boy, he's a young, young man. Swing like mad. I could still, right now, I could see him as if it was yesterday. Just as delicate as he could have played. Well, those guys, he's creative. That's one thing. I never tried to break my head to go and try to do what they were doing. And still, if they were doing, they still are doing. They are creators. They made it possible for all planet players. And it would be sort of foolish for me to go and break my head trying to play like them. Yeah. I love clarinet. I would like to do that style, but I don't have, I don't think the way they think. I can't produce what those guys do.
Yeah, well, your style to me is more like Polo Barnes and George Lewis, the, on clarinet, I mean.
Well, I, as I said, I would like, I loved their style, but I couldn't play what they played.
Yeah. The memory of those guys sort of went, was going through you when you were picking up the instrument,

right? I couldn't forget it. I couldn't forget it. Yeah. I couldn't forget it. Impossible. Because those guys, they, they played it at nobody else. They, they're the creators of, of, of, of jazz, and, and you can't get around it. There's nobody ever played like they played then and what they are playing today. Nobody may ever again. No. Well, the future we can't tell, but for sure nobody have done it. Yeah. Yeah. Now you take Sidney Baxter, if you picture what he played at that time and what Sidney was playing when I left Europe to come to San Francisco, it's terrific. Now you don't try to break your head, play the blues like Sidney Baxter, and everything else that he played, well, you'd be an old man and you'd never do it. Yeah. Because that's another creator. I don't think, nobody can play the blues like Sidney Baxter played. Yeah. I don't think so.

Well, the, the horn practically blew up in his hands, so. Great man. Uh, you were telling me when you were over there, let's see, this would be, uh, oh, a long time later, uh, that, uh, I always got the impression when I hear him that, my God, he frightened you to death to be in the same room with him. Is that so? To you?

Did you ever get that impression? Of, uh, of Sidney? Yeah. Well, Sidney, I knew Sidney since, uh, I think 27 or 29, when he left Germany to go back to France. He was in Germany at that time. And I, I've lost a job in Brechtop on the Carlos Sidney Baxter. When Baxter came from Germany, jazz had changed in Germany, you see, and as he, as he couldn't read, he got it sort of hard because he couldn't change his style, didn't know the Martin Nogues that was coming out. And so he had it at the time kind of hard, became the past. And I met him, and, uh, Brechtop knew him in New York, you see. Who is he? So, that's where I met Sidney. And, uh, I found out that Brechtop wanted to get rid of me to take him. Hmm. And when I came back the first night, I heard it, you know, on the QT, and the next night I went to work, but with a feeling that I was going to lose my job still. And so, I heard Sidney playing, he sat in my place, and it was too bad, I think. It was too much what he played. So I could understand that she wanted to take him. So, when I found out the next night, she even went and got, uh, they call it, Vissier in French. It's another man that comes, and he's, uh, going to the government, you know, everything, he sees what he says, that's the law, and, uh, that's it. So she had this man to come there to, while I rest, I go to the bar. And I was at the bar, and I was at the bar when the man came in, because I was taking a break. And she said, you see, this man is not doing his work here at the bar. And the man says, yes, I'm here to take notes of you. You're not only a good wife, isn't it? Yes. I said, Brechtop. He says, come here, let me tell you something. I was expecting, uh, to take this job tonight. I said, you could have saved yourself 50 francs. Because she had paid 50 francs to have this man to come up and verify that I was on the, you know, not on my job. And I said, you could have saved him 50 francs. I said, you could have saved him 50 francs. I can't play like Sidney, by the shit, and I can understand if you want him. And so you could have saved yourself that 50 francs. I said, he can have the job now. He said, she looked at me funny. And everybody. Because I just figured that if you want to do something, go ahead and do it. I'm going to get out of your way. I don't believe in staying in anybody's way. And Sidney heard about it, and he talked to me about it. He says, you know, that's not my fault. I said, Sidney, I don't care whose fault it is. You deserve the job.
Yeah.
Because you're the best man, and that's all it's to it. Yeah. And we became friends from that time on.
You've got to get a lot of chumming.

Yes. We became close friends together ever since. And when Sidney came back to Paris the last time after the war, I was accepted in his room when nobody else could come up there with a walk above a few. There was one, just one, just one. One. The position that was able to see when I announced my name in the hotel where he was staying, he says, yes, let him come up. Yeah. Just like that. And I went up. The only one he never had up. Spent five hours with him talking. Talking down to me. Five hours. He told me everything about his life. Yeah. And I was there when he left before the war to go, come back to the state. Yeah. See, he had a little trouble there in Paris. I don't know if you've heard about it. No. You've never heard about it? No.
Not in any of the details.

Well, I was there when it happened and he had to leave and I had to bring that up, but it's the truth anyway. The truth can be put on that. It's living. And when he came back, he, ten years after that, he came back and he, when he went, when he got out and I wanted to help him. He said, if you need anything, just let me know. And he never forget that he saw that. I really meant to be in his corner and be his friend. You know? And that's why he received me when he came back. Oh, yeah. Ten years after. I never known Sidney. Been very close to him. I made some recording with him, I think. No, but Sissy. What do you want with him? Some records with Sisley? Sisley.
Sisley. Yeah. No, not with Sidney. Oh, I thought Sidney was a good one. I was a good one. I was a good one.
I was a good one.
Sidney. Oh, I thought Sidney was in that.
In one. No. That was Sidney that was in 29. Yeah. Or 30 or 31 somewhere.
Oh, you made some black stick in some of those. You were on Alba Sax, were you? Or...
Yes.
Yeah. That's right.
Alba Sax. But Sidney was with Noble before then. I think Sidney, John Noble, Sissel, I think in 28, oh 27, 90, somewhere long there anyway.
Were you in Paris when Lizzie Miles was there? Yes. You were? Wasn't she called the Black Rose in Paris? Something like that.

I knew all those artists that came over. One is in, I can't remember their name, Elizabeth Wells. Did you do any blonde with, any groups with her? Well, in nightclubs I played with Elizabeth Wells. You never heard of Florence Mill? Yeah. Well, I met her too when she came to Europe. I think it was in the same outfit that Esham Joan was with. Johnny Dunn came over.
Johnny Dunn, there was that swinging cat. Yes.
Did you play with him? I met him. Well, and I didn't play with him, but I heard him play. He had that long trumpet, you know. He was a good showman. He was a good showman.
I prize those records I've got of him and Garvin Bouchelle on clarinet. Yeah. Yeah. Did you keep in touch with Hotline Records or what, the scene over here? Because you've heard of these guys.
Well, I used to belong to the, while I was over there, I belonged to the Hot Club of France and was traveling. Was that Pernacier's?
Was that Pernacier's deal? Yes. Pernacier.
Yeah.
Pernacier. And Pierre Nourie.
Oh, yeah. Pierre Nourie, the women Pernacier, is the one that started the Hot Club of France. And so I used to go to the house and listen to the ladies and things they had.
And so, you certainly had an odd life. I mean, it's been different.
Me?
Yeah. Well, yes. It's a... I mean, a lot of guys did the traveling, but not like that, you know. You pulled out of there right when the war came for Brazil.
Yes.
Yeah.
I never did follow the gang. Yeah. I'm not a gang man.
Yeah.

If I were to go anywhere, I just make up my mind whether I can go there or not, and I'll take the chance. And go, and that's why I went to Europe. And on those conditions, I thought I was in conditions, you know, able, able, my ability would allow me to go over and make it. And I realized that when I got in Paris, it was really amazing to see in two months' time, I was known in Paris, because I brought that New Orleans style on trumpet, which no one was doing.
Oh, yeah.

The real thing, yeah. Yes. And then I stayed around there, and I saw, I wanted to play clannery, and I saw the trumpet was coming out of style, and my teeth was getting bad, too. Yeah. So I've learned clannery. That's caused me learning clannery. Because all the cabarets in Paris was changing to three tenors, two guitars, bass, and violin, piano. Yeah. And there was so much white there. It says, why hang on, Dixieland style, or jazz, and style, or go in and to play what style was in? You see, that's how Sydney got it so bad at one time, because style really changed in Paris. And Paris is the key of Europe. Yeah. You see, what Paris do, Berlin will do, Rome will do. Yeah. You see, Brussels, Amsterdam, all those.
Did you do traveling in Europe yourself, as a musician? Oh, yes. I went in everybody's country. Did you? But no, I didn't, Scandinavian. Straight music?

Straight music, or did you play jazz in these other countries? Well, I always did play, as much as I was left, swing and jazz, you see. If I had a tiny space, I'd come out with something. Yeah. But a lot of times I played with big bands, and I didn't stay with them because it was too strict. You see, I had to play even too sweet. And when you play swing, well, you'll play four bars, six bars, eight bars, and once a night you may take 32 bars. Yeah. And that wasn't enough.
I think some, the German label Telephumpen produced some of your records. Yes, I have. Big Boy Boogie, and they re-released them or something in there. Did you record one?

Well, I recorded in Berlin in 53, and I was very disappointed. I've made one record with, you know, Frank Burley's blues or something. Yeah. And the other side, I forgot what it was. And I talked to the trumpet player that was supposed to make this record for me. I told him why they wanted it, and why we should have put on the wax was that. Well, he had never made no recording. He was very obedient for those, that first section of one, two sides. And after they put out that record, they sold it overnight in Berlin and in Frankfurt and all over the time. And overnight it was gone. Yeah. They called me up to make some more records. But more sides, I think, but six sides at that time. So I talked to this guy, and he made up his mind. He wanted to play like Raul Aldrich played or play like Harry Jane played. And I said, they don't want that. Yeah. They want you to play like Bong Johnson. They want you to play like Tommy Latna. Those, that's the style they want, because he knew of those two. Yeah. They don't even want Louis Armstrong style. They had enough of that anyway on record. Yes. So they want something like Tommy Latna. Oh, that's what they want. Yes. And we got on the record, they start goofing. So I made them just to make them. I knew I was not going to do anymore. You see? And I made them, and they came out. I just played them, and it was just to finish with them. Oh, yeah. And I told them to do contract over, and I told them I would do it. Because it's bad, it was bad for me, you know, because I couldn't play. I can't play when I'm dissatisfied. Yeah. You know. So I continued to make those records out of the roof, you know. And I would continue with that same band anyway.
It wasn't until you came around here, was it, that you tried to not restore, but find that New Orleans element in your clarinet. Well, yes.

When I came back, I had to do a lot of things. And I never did want to listen too much at record to copy anybody first, because I realized I can't do what they do, as I mentioned before. Yeah. So what I had to do was close my eyes and picture all those famous guys, especially as I've worked with Frank Matthew for a long time. And I knew how he played, and I still couldn't picture, you know, dogs when I heard him and hear different clarinet players from New Orleans that even wasn't known. And I had to picture all that, you know. Concentrate. And I had to really change my style here to get into jazz. Yeah.

Well, these guys like, these guys like Milky, I think, escaped Frank what so many old fake cats have done. Milky seems to play a more, shall we say, more real, earthy trombones, the real thing, because he isn't imitating. You understand? Yes. He's playing the New Orleans idiom, but he's not imitating.
Yes. That's, that has, that has helped me a lot. Yeah. Him and, and, and Patton.
Yeah.

PT. It's almost like listening to the real thing, don't you hear them? Yes. That, they have, have a lot, very, very, they have a lot of great help. And, and with this guy on banjo, Jack Dick Armstrong, if you have it, it's easy, it makes it so easy for you to play. Yeah. You know, you know, you've got solid rhythm, correct chords, and you don't have to worry.
You know, he's come a long way on banjo, when he first started, he was draggy.
Yeah. Yeah. You know, no more. No. I can get so, I can't play with anybody on banjo, you know.
I like that trio sound anyway, the, about the best of all. Yeah. Yeah, that trio. And then something, with Erickson. Yeah. He's a wild, wild piano player. Yeah.

So, you see the environment, I was lucky to fill in with Bob, and Parkstock, and Erickson, and I was three all the keys, and I was lucky to fill in with them. Yeah. And it helped me a lot, so I'm telling you.
I think Milky could be a great trombonist if you wanted to be.
Yeah, well, he should, I mean, he's good, there's no doubt about it. And if you don't seem to want to put the time...

Yeah. And concentration, and he should, but I don't think he should let himself go, because he has lots to offer, you see. And he should let himself go. That's neglectful. Like all musicians will do, let himself go, because he says, well, I...

Well, they give up hope. They think it's something that isn't, you see. Like you were mentioning, it's best to have a trade and use it as a paying application. Yes. Something you love, and if they give money, okay.
Yes.
I think Mielke's going to have to make this adjustment. All of them.
Yes, because he plays too much horn, and he should. And he's not a good trombone player.
Same with Burt, that so-called security puts him in a rut, you see, like Bale's.

Yes. But Bale, now for me, they say there's a lot of piano players around here that plays better than him. I will not agree. They may bang the piano differently than he does. Yeah. But I think, but I know he is first a musician, and second a piano player. And he has started piano because from the tone that he gets on the piano, that's what he is. Just like Bale's. He knows. Yes. He knows how to play piano.
You see?

He gets a tone on piano. He gets, and when he plays, he interprets, he has a lot of interpretation in his playing. He's not brought to, and he can be if he wants to. Yeah. But I think- Like you said, he's a solid interpreter. Yeah, he's a little interpreter in here.
Yeah, so jazz. I think he's the last of the great band pianists. He is.
And there's trombones around here that will eventually make it if he was to continue at it. It's that guy, Ben Dean Lee. Oh, yeah.
I really like his style.

He swings, and he's so original, you see, but it looks like he doesn't play enough, or doesn't practice enough, or doesn't help. I don't know. He should, him too, he shouldn't let himself go. Yeah. He should continue, because he has something also to offer. And this other trombone player, what is his name? Yeah. The blades around here.
The legs are so straight. Tall guy? No. Oh, yeah. Now I know who you talk about. I don't know his name.
Well, he's, he's quite well considered here in the city. Yeah. Very well considered.
I was, uh, going to ask you something. Did you hear Ori when he was down there? I mean, in the 20s? Never. Never did hear him? Never. Never.
I heard Ori here in San Francisco.
It's funny.

He should, I think he should hire you. Because it's, uh, it's, uh, every time where he went, I was somewhere else, and when I went there, he was going someplace else. Yeah. Well, I tell you, you said he should hire me.

Well, I think you and Andy Blakeney. Have you heard of Blakeney? No. He plays trumpet somewhat like, uh, you know, Bunk. Mm-hmm. And, uh, he's got him. You see they have an underground in L.A. Colored Thaws do.
Yeah.

And, uh, they're playing some good, doing his jazz, but, of course, uh, the old faith people don't know about it. They screwed up if they did. It's just for their own Johnny St. Cyr, uh, Mon Toody Garland, the bass player. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
